changes.before: Complete restoreMatches(expected, restored). Both inputs have version and notes arrays of {id,title}. Expected IDs are unique. Return true only when versions and every ID/title pair match, ignoring row order. Both inputs are well-formed records under this contract.
changes.after: Check the contents of restored data. A file name or matching row count cannot prove the data is right.

before: A backup file existing is not proof that it can restore the required data.
A restore drill opens the saved copy in an isolated environment and checks meaningful records and schema expectations.
Comparing only row counts can miss changed or replaced data. Two different sets of notes can have the same count.
Compare stable IDs and their values. Database query order is not guaranteed unless requested, so sort copies before comparing.

Use copied arrays when sorting so verification does not rearrange the caller’s records.

For numeric IDs, [...rows].sort((left, right) => left.id - right.id) orders a copy from smallest ID to largest. After checking equal lengths, compare each corresponding pair's ID and title. every((row, index) => condition) returns true only if the condition holds for every row; index identifies the matching position in the other array.
The supplied Python companion creates a disposable SQLite backup, closes the source, reopens the backup, and checks integrity plus known rows.
It never reads or overwrites your real files. Production recovery also needs retention, access controls, encryption where appropriate, and a tested recovery process.
after: A backup is a saved copy of data. Restoring means reading that copy so the app can use the data again.
A restore drill tries this in a separate, safe place. It checks that the saved copy opens and contains the needed records.
Two lists can have the same number of notes but different titles. Check the actual values as well as the count.
An ID identifies a note. Match each ID with its title. Ignore row order: a database can return the same rows in a different order.

Complete restoreMatches(expected, restored). Check equal versions and lengths. Sort a copy of each notes array by numeric ID. Then compare the ID and title at each matching position. Copying first keeps the original arrays in their original order.
The downloadable Python companion makes a temporary SQLite database and backup. It closes the source, opens the backup, and checks its stored rows and database integrity.

The browser checks the supplied snapshots. The companion tests a disposable backup. Neither checks a backup of your own app. A real recovery plan must also check the other data and settings that app needs.

before.question: The restored database has the expected two rows, but one note title is wrong. Is comparing only the row count enough evidence of a correct restore?
choices: Yes; equal counts prove equal data.
No; verify important identities and values as well.
Yes; a backup extension guarantees its contents.
before.explanation: Counts cannot distinguish different content of the same size. A restore check should test the data the application depends on.

after.question: A restored copy has two rows as expected, but one title is wrong. Is checking only the count enough?
choices: Yes. Equal counts prove the data matches.
No. Check the IDs and their values too.
Yes. The file's name proves its contents.
after.explanation: Two lists can have the same size and different contents. A restore check must check the data the app needs.

changes.before: The browser verifies supplied snapshot data only. The companion Python script separately demonstrates a real disposable SQLite backup/reopen; neither step proves a production backup has been made or that all possible corruption is detected.
changes.after: The browser compares well-formed snapshots with numeric IDs; expected IDs are unique. The separate Python companion uses disposable SQLite files. Passing these checks does not verify a production backup or detect every possible problem.
